questions.title: Molds feeding on dead matter are saprophytes
questions.question: The molds obtained nutrition from dead and decaying matter which are called ?

explanations.A: Correct. Organisms, including moulds, that feed on dead animal or plant material and thereby decompose it are called saprophytes. Saprophytes are free-living decomposers, not organisms dependent on a living host. This decomposer role is the defining feature of a saprophyte.
explanations.B: Incorrect. A parasite depends on a living host for nutrition, typically at the host's expense -- the reverse of feeding on dead, decaying matter.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A commensal lives in or on a living host without harming it, benefiting from that living association -- not from decomposing dead matter.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since "saprophytes" correctly names organisms feeding on dead and decaying matter, "none of these" is wrong.

questions.title: This source's printed answer for the majority-of-bacteria question
questions.question: Majority of bacteria are ?

explanations.A: Incorrect per this source's printed key. Saprophytes -- free-living organisms decomposing dead organic matter -- are, by standard microbiology teaching, the majority ecological category of bacteria in nature; this source's own printed answer names Parasites instead.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Symbionts (organisms in a mutually beneficial relationship with a host) are not the printed majority category here.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Commensals (organisms benefiting from a host without helping or harming it, as with much of the normal flora) are not the printed majority category here either.
explanations.D: Correct per this source's printed answer key. This bank's own plain-text ANSWERS table keys "Parasites" as the majority ecological category of bacteria. The key is followed as printed, per the lane's standing rule. This runs against the more commonly taught view that saprophytes, not parasites, make up the majority of bacteria in nature -- see author_notes for that doubt.

questions.author_notes: Printed key (D, Parasites) is doubtful against the standard microbiology/parasitology teaching that the majority of bacteria in nature are saprophytic (free-living decomposers), with only a minority being pathogenic parasites -- the same distinction this pass's own Q159 and this MUST concept both draw. However, no other item in this source (chapter 1 or elsewhere read so far) states the opposite outright, so the bank shows no internal inconsistency about this specific claim; per the lane's standing rule, the printed key stands and is authored as printed, with this doubt recorded here as a held-printed-key-conflict candidate for Omar to review against the source or an official answer sheet, rather than held outright.
